units.text: What happens if the source accepts a bad change? Replication can faithfully carry corruption to another Region. In S three, delete-marker replication depends on configuration; the principle is that a second online copy is not necessarily a clean restore point.

Keep prior versions or protected points and test access to them. When you investigate an incident, locate a known-good point before the damaging change and restore it. Faster replication limits lag; it does not give you a historical recovery guarantee.

For R D S and Aurora, compare snapshots with a point-in-time restore to a new target where supported. Dynamo D B point-in-time recovery creates a new table; global tables are for multi-Region operation and do not themselves rewind an erroneous write.

An S three object version is not a transactionally consistent database restore. For S three, recover the appropriate version or an eligible replica after checking what was actually copied. Match the recovery mechanism to the unit you need back.

For D N S failover, the decision is made when Route 53 answers a query. In this example the primary is unhealthy and the recovery endpoint is healthy, so new answers select the recovery record. Test the application and its dependencies, not just that its listener is reachable.

Clients can retain the previous answer until they ask again. Existing sessions are separate. Test the actual time until users are served successfully, rather than calling the moment a health check changes the recovery time.

Think of Global Accelerator as a stable network entry point. A standard accelerator can redirect new flows toward healthy endpoints without asking clients to learn a new public address. It does not move the state of an already established connection.

Before relying on that shift, check that the destination has current data, sufficient capacity, and an appropriate session strategy. Network failover steers a connection; it does not rebuild the application that receives it.

ARC routing controls are separate from application probes. A routing-control state changes the associated Route 53 health signal, while safety rules can guard against unsafe combinations. Preconfigure and rehearse the controls before the disrupted Region is needed.

When responders verify recovery readiness, they can shift the intended regional traffic according to the runbook. Route 53 still provides the D N S response; ARC is a control, not a proxy in the request path.

Here the recovery boundary is one Availability Zone, not another Region. ARC changes routing for a supported resource so new connections can avoid the affected zone. It is not a network hop, and existing connections may continue until clients reconnect.
Check that the remaining zones can carry the load. Zonal shift does not restore corrupted data or make a failed Region available, so keep the recovery plan for those failures separate.

A recovery cluster needs images, workload definitions, network access, secrets, capacity and state. Replicating the image solves only one of those. Deploy and test the recovery workloads against the intended data before accepting traffic.

Use a representative transaction to prove that the new cluster can reach its dependencies and serve the load. An available control plane or a running container alone is not proof of application recovery.

Resilience Hub compares the modeled application against its resilience policy. Use estimated recovery targets and recommendations to decide what to fix. Treat the estimate as analysis, not as a measurement from a real outage.
After improving backup or recovery configuration, reassess. Then run a recovery test and compare observed behavior with the objectives; both the estimate and the drill can reveal a gap.

Convert the plan into a runbook with checked inputs, approved roles and a deliberate human gate when required. Verify each result before proceeding. An automatic rollback only happens if the runbook includes and can execute that branch.
Record the outcome, actions and verification evidence for the incident owner. An automation run that finished without errors is not the same as an application that met its recovery objectives.

Start with a hypothesis about a workload you are authorized to test. Set a bounded environment, an observable steady-state signal, and a stop threshold. A CloudWatch alarm can stop an A W S Fault Injection Service experiment when that threshold is reached.

Compare observed user impact with the hypothesis and verify recovery. If the evidence differs, improve the system or runbook. The point is learning whether the workload tolerates the failure, not simply that an experiment ran.
Log when impact began, when the incident was declared, and when recovery actions completed. A traffic change or a green dashboard gives a checkpoint; it is not automatically the time users recovered.
Measure actual loss using the latest recovered committed data and downtime using a representative service transaction. Compare those observations against the agreed R P O and R T O.

In a regional incident, confirm the failure using independent signals and name the recovery destination. The runbook can prime the routing control, but do not direct user traffic there until you have checked secondary data, capacity and the application path.

Execute the agreed traffic change, then test complete user journeys and capture the recovery measures. Do not reopen normal operations because a D N S answer changed; verify the workload can serve its users.

Contain the compromised identity and choose a protected recovery point known to predate the damage. Restore into an isolated recovery environment so teams can inspect it without exposing the original or the restored system to production traffic.

Check that the restored data and application behave as expected. Rotate affected secrets and verify logging and access as required. Restore production traffic only after approval, so a successful restore does not automatically reconnect a compromised path.

Choose by the job you must do. A W S Backup provides recovery points; Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates server disks. Route 53 selects D N S records and ARC manages preconfigured traffic control. Resilience Hub assesses the design and Fault Injection Service tests a controlled hypothesis. None replaces all the others.

Before calling a workload ready, confirm objectives, isolation, protected copies, infrastructure definitions, quotas and an approved runbook. Each item needs evidence you can recheck, not just a label on a diagram.

Test the path into recovery and the planned fallback. Record the actual timings, identify who owns each decision, and verify data and a real user transaction. If the rehearsal misses a target, the readiness checklist tells you what to repair next.
